# 16-pairio — sources

Back-test entry `16-pairio.yaml`: Pairio, a voice assistant that helps factory technicians fix broken machines (YC
Spring 2026, P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named
(the launch-era site is in German; its quotes are given in German, with the author's English in brackets). "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-04-21 and the weeks around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era where one
exists; anything later is marked as later).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Pairio – Fix broken equipment in factories faster", 2026-04-21 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Q18-pairio-fix-broken-equipment-in-factories-faster

- [FAQ] pairio.com FAQ, read 2026-10-22 — https://pairio.com/faq/
- [REF] pairio.com customer reference (Knipping), read 2026-10-22; figures "supplied by Knipping" — https://pairio.com/customer-references/

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Maintenance technicians and operators who fix machines on the production line.
   [LYC] "Pairio helps technicians and operators resolve faults faster with voice AI." [YCP] "AI mobile app that helps
   factory technicians fix broken machines". → `roles[technician]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: the
   technician only (operators are named too, but the fix and the report are the technician's).

2. **What (the job).** Get the machine running again fast, and keep the fix for the next person.
   [LYC] "Unplanned equipment downtime costs global industries over $1.4 trillion every year – and the root cause isn't
   broken machines. It's broken knowledge transfer." [LYC] "With the average technician in the US now 50 years old,
   knowledge is literally walking out the door". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the machine, when it fails, and afterwards when the fix should be written down.
   [LYC] "When a machine fails, resolution speed depends almost entirely on whether the one guy who's seen this before is
   working that day"; "Valuable technical clues are buried somewhere across 400 pages of OEM manuals or locked in outdated
   software"; "After spending 6 hours getting the line back up, the last thing a technician does is sit down and write a
   detailed fault report to institutionalize their knowledge". [FAQ] "Fundamentals and practical ways to use Pairio in
   day-to-day maintenance work." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: machine breakdown`. Author's choice: the window
   {5, WORKING_DAYS} (a working-day rhythm) and Frequency 2 to 4 working days out of 5 -- daily for the team, not for
   each technician (header); Prevalence `p_80_100`.

4. **Which people.** Technicians at US plants that keep their own maintenance team.
   [LYC] "Ask: Can you introduce us to plant and maintenance managers at US manufacturing firms?" [WB] "Pairio richtet sich
   an Unternehmen mit eigener Instandhaltung - vom Mittelstand bis zum Konzern." [Pairio is for companies with their own
   maintenance, from mid-sized firms to groups.] → `context.segment`, `market: US`; the German plants are in the header.

5. **Who pays.** The plant; the maintenance manager chooses, the plant manager agrees.
   [LYC] "If you know anyone in plant operations or maintenance in US manufacturing we'd love to talk with them". [WB]
   quotes a "Meister & Abteilungsleiter Instandhaltung" [foreman and head of maintenance] as a user. → `persona.
   decision_maker: {role: manager}`; Buyer and payer tests "The plant manager" (listed with "The IT department"):
   author's choice, no source names who signs. Purchase friction's tested item, "Connecting it to SAP or Maximo": [FAQ]
   "including systems such as SAP, IFS, IBM Maximo, Oracle EAM Cloud, Hexagon, SharePoint, Outlook, and Asset API"; [WB]
   "Die genaue Anbindung hängt von Ihrer IT-Landschaft ab." [The exact connection depends on your IT landscape.] The IT
   security review and the plant-wide rollout sign-off are the author's. Commitment's step, "run a pilot on one
   production line": [REF] "A clearly scoped pilot creates evidence"; "Following a two-month pilot, the solution was
   integrated in four weeks." (later than launch; the launch-era site offers "Kostenlose Demo" [free demo]).

6. **Mechanism.** Ask by voice or photo; answers from the manuals and past repairs; speak the fix, get a report.
   [LYC] "Simply ask and instantly receive any available technical clue"; "Speak and let Pairio structure their learnings
   into reusable know-how"; "Use photos and videos to capture even more contextual knowledge". [WB] "Sprache, Foto oder
   Video rein - fertiger Bericht raus" [voice, photo or video in, finished report out]; "Pairio erkennt Fehlerbild,
   Maßnahmen, Ersatzteile und erstellt einen strukturierten Bericht." [Pairio recognises the fault, the actions, the spare
   parts and writes a structured report.] [YCP] "Users just take a picture of the broken machine and we search thousands
   of pages of manuals to find the right solution." → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`; Compatibility (a phone
   allowed at the machine — tested; manuals as files; quiet enough to speak) and Adoption friction (speak the fix when
   done — tested; photograph the fault first) are the author's, from the mechanism's own needs and [BLOG] ("tools that fit
   how technicians actually work, on mobile, in loud environments"). Relative advantage: shorter_time from [WB] "-25%
   MTTR", less_help_needed from [LYC]'s "the one guy who's seen this before"; the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** No price public; the cost is technician time.
   [WB] "Kostenlose Demo" and "Demo buchen" [free demo; book a demo], no price; [SITE] "Book a free demo", no price.
   → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $600 to $1,200 per technician a year is **the operator's reading** (about $50 to
   $100 a seat a month; header). Existing sacrifice, HOURS 150 to 300 of the breakdowns per technician a year: author's
   arithmetic -- 3 to 6 hours a week of a technician's time lost to hunting through manuals, waiting for the one person
   who knows, extra trips for tools and parts, and the report written afterwards, over about 50 working weeks; the scale
   is set by [LYC]'s "6 hours getting the line back up" and by [WB]'s "-25% MTTR" and "-80% Ablageaufwand" (the shares
   the company says it removes). The rate, $31 an hour, is [BLS] "$30.82 per hour" (May 2025 median), the author's
   stand-in. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [BLOG] "At a specialty manufacturer in Illinois, the maintenance team told me some shifts run with a single
   technician."; "The troubleshooting descriptions? Consistently useless. 'Reset machine.' 'Machine broken, fixed it.'
   'Called supplier.'"; "The work order says there's a problem with the injection molding machine. That's it. They show
   up, assess, go back for parts, come back again."; "When a conveyor goes down, every minute counts in a way that's
   directly visible to the customer."; "she'd watched a technician try to use ChatGPT out of desperation to solve a
   machine-specific problem."

respondent carries the name of a customer, technician or founder in the sources.

## Status today

Same idea. [SITE] (English, 2026-10-22) describes the same assistant (fault reports, manual search, data analysis, work
instructions) now aimed at US plants, with the Knipping reference: [REF] "Knipping reduced mean time to repair (MTTR) by
25%, generated €500K in savings through avoided downtime, and achieved a 95% adoption rate." and "Four German locations
are already onboarded." [FAQ] "In suitable use cases, MTTR can be reduced by up to 25%, filing effort by up to 80%, and
onboarding time by up to 90%." Price today: still not public ("Book a free demo").

## Could not be sourced

- **Any price.** Nothing public at launch or today; the founder's price is the operator's reading (header, item 7), so the
  Price line measures that reading, not the company's price.
- **A per-plant money cost.** Only the global $1.4 trillion is public; the chain cost is the technicians' time instead
  (header).
- **The hours per technician a year.** The sources give one example (6 hours on one breakdown) and shares removed; the
  150 to 300 is the author's arithmetic.
- **A technician's hour.** [BLS]'s median stands in.
- **Who signs, and the purchase steps.** No source names the buyer above the maintenance manager; the plant manager, the
  IT department, the security review and the rollout sign-off are the author's (the SAP or Maximo connection is sourced).
- **How often one technician meets a breakdown.** "Day-to-day" is the team's rhythm; the 2 to 4 working days out of 5 is
  the author's.
- **First-person technician accounts.** No Launch HN or forum thread; the occasions are scripted from [BLOG] (the
  founder's own account of US visits) and [WB]'s two user quotes ("Mit der App kann ich alles direkt dokumentieren und
  muss mir keine Sorgen machen, dass ich etwas vergesse." [With the app I can document everything straight away and
  needn't worry about forgetting something.]).

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem to sending, but the recency question at screen 4 splits the two context screens, and it would fit better after screen 5, once the context is fully defined.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same question word for word ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'), though the flow doesn't show their fields, so I can only judge the wording.
founder.missing: Nothing asks about what Pairio does (voice or photo in, answers from manuals and past repairs, finished fault report out), whether a technician can use a phone and speak at the machine, what it costs, or who pays: the technician uses it, but the maintenance manager chooses and the plant pays, so the technicians can't answer for the purchase. PRIMARY.order_why: It starts with whether my plant fits, moves to whether and how often I needed the one coworker who knew the fault, then goes on to what I'd want easier and how my last breakdown went, which is a natural order.

screens.why1: Right after I said how technicians get a machine running today, it is obvious why Keel now asks how well that way works, and this is the last check of the problem step.
screens.why2: The rows are shop-floor plain, but in a plant 'the order and the line stay fixed' reads like a production line and a repair until a second read shows it means the list and the bar.
screens.why3: I know from plant visits how these breakdowns go, and a technician can say from the last week whether the fix came straight away, took hours or waited for someone.
screens.why4: The scale runs in a sensible order, but hours of asking can overlap with waiting for the person who knows, and there is no row for a known fix held up by a part or for a machine fixed with no record left.
screens.why5: The asking and the OEM manuals are kept, but the rows drop the record half of my job, and the saved bar still names 'Found it, logged a line or two' while the box names 'The fix was found after a short search'.

screens.why1: The questions are checked and the study is about to go out, so choosing who asks them is the obvious next step before people see it.
screens.why2: The choice itself is plain, but the hint packs in video, typing or tapping, one-time recording, 400 credits and text-message links, so I need a second read to see what I am deciding and paying for.
screens.why3: I can hear both voices and pick the one I think suits my technicians, but it is a taste guess because nothing tells me which one a technician on a loud plant floor would answer more readily.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers, each with a five-second sample and Daphne preselected, are complete and distinct, and a choice this simple needs no escape chip.
screens.why5: "Maintenance technicians" is kept and nothing of my product leaks, but the screen talks only of voice and hearing while the interviewer appears on video, so I cannot tell whether I am also choosing the face I will lock and record.
screens.instead: Who should ask maintenance technicians your questions on video? Watch each 5-second sample; recording your pick costs 400 credits either way. Options: Daphne (picked for you) / Saskia.

screens.why1: Just before sending the study, it is obvious why I must choose how my technicians will answer it, right after choosing who asks them.
screens.why2: The choice is clear to me, but "Still recording · ready in a few minutes" and "Ready when Daphne is" take a second read because they could be about the interview rather than her voice sample being prepared.
screens.why3: I know technicians work on phones on loud floors and may answer between jobs, so I can choose from what I know, and the stated accuracy where it is loud speaks directly to that.
screens.why4: AI interviewer, read and tap, or the respondent's choice are distinct and complete options for how technicians could answer, and no escape chip is needed for this founder's setup choice.
screens.why5: The screen keeps my word "maintenance technicians", changes nothing I typed, and does not put my product in front of a respondent.
screens.instead: Keep the question and options, but replace the status lines with "Daphne's voice sample ready in a few minutes" and, for the third option, "Ready once Daphne's voice sample is done".

screens.why1: Right after choosing how technicians will answer, the obvious last step before sending is deciding who gets the link, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: "Who gets a link?" and the three options read cleanly on first pass; "Contacts page" is Keel's own word but is explained well enough by "From a search".
screens.why3: As the founder I know whether I am sending to plant and maintenance contacts by name, searching for them, or posting in a group, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: Named people, people found through Keel and an open link in a group are distinct, cover how I would reach technicians, and each says plainly what happens next.
screens.why5: The screen is about distribution and changes nothing I typed; my pick of people I know by name is kept as the first option.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right under the title with its deciding number beside it (Frequency: 4 answered), and the card adds that 5 are needed, though the line names only Frequency when Importance and Current solution are short too.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart here, only tally lines; '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar' reads at once, but I need a second look to see why only 4 of the 7 count on the other three cards when 6 said yes.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked, Importance and Current solution word for word, and the problem statement above them is my own launch story about the one person who has seen the fault and knowledge walking out the door.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I should get more answers, but the page never says so, how many more people to send it to, or what one holding card and three open ones mean for Pairio.
screens.why_b5: Nothing overreaches: 7 people stays visible, the 4-answer cards are refused a call, and Prevalence is only 'Holding up', marked as exactly at the bar rather than strong.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of your 4 beliefs have 4 answers and need 5, so send the study to more technicians who had a breakdown this week; so far only Prevalence holds, at the bar with 6 of 7.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar", so I get both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The strip counts people who said yes, across 7 cells, with the marker at 6, so what is counted, how many people and where the bar sits are all plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: "Prevalence" and "need the only coworker who knew the fault" are recognisably my "one guy who's seen this before", but the wording is stiff and this isn't one of the beliefs I remember checking on the way in, which were about manuals and current fixes.
screens.why_b4: The So line correctly sends me to how often and whether it matters, but it doesn't say what this result means for my idea or that one fewer yes would have missed the bar.
screens.why_b5: It keeps the 7 visible, limits the claim to "among these 7", says "a lean, not a call" and admits the result is exactly at the bar, so nothing overreaches.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 6 of 7 needed the one coworker who knew the fault this week, and one fewer yes would miss your bar; the need for that person looks common, but only the next two cards can show whether it is frequent and painful enough to build on.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" is stated at the top with the deciding number right under it, 4 against the 5 needed, and the So line repeats it, so I know it is no call and why.
screens.why_b2: The axis of working days, the median at 1 and the bar of 3 of 4 are all drawn, but I need a second look at "beyond, the good side" and at how a strip with a bar at 3 relates to my 2-to-4 range and to the empty fifth cell.
screens.why_b3: "Frequency" and my 2-to-4 days are recognisable, and "the only coworker who knew the fault" is my "one guy who's seen this before", though it is stiffly reworded and I would not say it that way to a technician.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is a generic line: it doesn't tell me to get at least one more countable technician, or what it means for my idea that three of the four counted needed that coworker less often than I said.
screens.why_b5: It overclaims nothing and says the group is small, but the verdict's "4 answered" contradicts the count line's "6 answered, 4 counted", which is a soft slip about who answered.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 6 answered, 4 could be counted, 5 are needed. So far only 1 of the 4 needed that coworker on 2 to 4 days and the middle answer is 1 day, so the lean is against you; get more technicians to answer before you lean on "the one guy" as a weekly pain.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" is plain and 5 needed is beside it, but the line under the verdict says 4 answered while the count line says 6 answered and 4 counted, so I have to stop and work out which number decides it.
screens.why_b2: The caption makes the picks and the 4 people clear, but the strip shows 3 for and 5 against in picks while the bar is 3 of 4 people, so it takes a second look to see that I am at the bar rather than well short of it.
screens.why_b3: Importance and the line about tracing a fault through buried manuals being one of the two are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" keeps me from acting on this, but it doesn't tell me to get more technicians counted or what to do meanwhile about spare parts and short-staffing, which also drew picks.
screens.why_b5: It makes no claim beyond these people and it says the group is small, but "4 answered" understates the 6 who did, and the 3-against-5 strip can read as a majority against me when 3 of 4 people picked my problem.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 6 answered, 4 counted, 5 needed. 3 of those 4 put buried manuals in their two, which is at your 2-in-3 bar, so get at least one more technician's clear answer before you rely on it; spare parts and short staffing each drew 2 picks, so ask about them too.

screens.why_b1: The verdict "Too few to call" sits directly above the number that decides it, 4 against the 5 needed, and the So line repeats both.
screens.why_b2: The categories, my line and the 3 of 4 at the bar are plain, but I need a second look to reconcile the "4 answered" under the verdict with "6 answered, 4 counted" and to see why a marker reached at 3 of 4 still makes no call.
screens.why_b3: The card's name and the belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in, including asking whoever has seen the fault or digging through OEM manuals and the "Found it, logged a line or two" bar.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" tells me not to act on it, and I can infer I need one more counted answer, but it never says to get that answer or what it would mean for the idea.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know no answer has been reached and why.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it makes sense to check that I work at a plant with its own maintenance crew before asking about my work.
screens.why2: A US plant with its own maintenance team is how I'd describe my shop, and I get it on one read, though a contractor might pause over it.
screens.why3: I know who I work for and that our plant keeps its own maintenance team, so I can answer without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, don't overlap, and a screener needs no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment almost word for word, and nothing about a product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, and two options are easy to hold on one hearing, even if 'I'll read 2 options' is a little stiff.

screens.why1: After asking if my plant runs its own maintenance team, asking about a recent breakdown makes sense, but it jumps straight to needing one particular coworker without first asking whether I had a machine down at all.
screens.why2: I know what a fault is, but "the only coworker who knew the fault" reads oddly on first pass, since a shop guy would say "the one guy who's seen this before" and the question never mentions a machine going down.
screens.why3: I know whether I had to track down or call the one guy who knew a problem this week, so I can answer it from my own last few shifts.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but there are two escapes where there should be one, "I'd rather not say" should not exist, and "I can't recall one particular machine down" is a clumsy sentence that doesn't match a question about a coworker.
screens.why5: No product leaks to me, but the question has narrowed getting a downed machine running again to needing one coworker, which assumes the answer and sits awkwardly with the next screen's plain "your last machine down."
screens.why6: It is short and easy to say as one yes-or-no question, but heard once, "the only coworker who knew the fault" is a clunky clause that I might have to ask to hear again.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did a machine go down that only one coworker knew how to fix? Yes or no.

screens.why1: I just said yes to needing that coworker, so asking how many days that happened is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I get it, but 'the only coworker who knew the fault' is stiff and not how I'd say it; I'd say 'the one guy who's seen this before', and it reads like one particular person when each breakdown could be a different guy.
screens.why3: I know which days this week I had to go find or call the guy who'd seen it before, so I can answer from memory.
screens.why4: One to five covers it after I've already said yes at least once, the numbers don't overlap, and 'I can't recall' fits as the way out.
screens.why5: No product or company leaks through, but 'knew the fault' sounds like somebody's written-up term rather than shop talk, so it has drifted a little from how a tech would put it.
screens.why6: It's one short question and 'a number from 1 to 5, or say you can't recall' is easy to hold and answer after hearing it once.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, on how many days did you need the one person who'd seen that breakdown before? A number from 1 to 5, or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: After being asked about needing the one coworker who knew the fault, it makes sense to ask what part of my week I would most want made easier.
screens.why2: I get all of it on first hearing except "buried manuals", which is a bit of a writer's phrase, since I'd say the manual is 400 pages or I can't find it in there.
screens.why3: Every one of these is part of my week on the floor, so I can pick from what actually happened.
screens.why4: The five are mostly distinct and None of these fits, but the fault option only covers manuals when my real problem is often getting hold of the guy who has seen it before, which is what the last two questions were about.
screens.why5: No product or company leaks to me, but "tracing a fault through buried manuals" sounds a little like someone's pitch rather than how a technician talks.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, and five short options I can hold in my head after hearing them once, with the one way out said last.
screens.instead: Think of your last working week on the plant floor. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Keeping up with planned maintenance; getting the right spare parts in time; finding out how to fix a fault; covering the shift with too few technicians; or working safely around running equipment. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: After asking how often I needed the one guy who knew the fault and what I'd want easier, asking how my last machine down actually went is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: OEM manuals and logged are shop words I use, but 'how did asking whoever has seen the fault before or digging through OEM manuals go' is a long either-or, and I'd have to read it twice to see it means both ways of chasing the fix.
screens.why3: I had a machine down recently and I know exactly how I chased the fix and what I wrote in the log.
screens.why4: The options mix two things, finding the fix and logging it, so 'waited for the one person who knew' and 'trial and error' say nothing about the log and could overlap with hunting through manuals, and there's no option for waiting and then logging it fine.
screens.why5: It stays on how we really get a machine back up and leave a record, and no product or company language reaches me.
screens.why6: The stem is one question and the list is short phrases I can hold, but 'asking whoever has seen the fault before or digging through OEM manuals' is a mouthful in one breath, and 'OEM' only works because I already know it.
screens.instead: Think of your last machine down. How did finding the fix go? Found it fast; found it after hunting through manuals; waited for the one person who knew; or trial and error while the line stayed down. Or say you can't recall.
